Learning Objectives
Review the origin of benign vascular tumors of bone.
Explain the epidemiology and etiology of benign vascular tumors of bone.
Identify the radiographic features of benign vascular tumors of bone.
Discuss the type and timing of management for benign vascular tumors of bone.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Benign vascular tumors of bone are collections of blood vessels formed in the intramedullary
canal or the cortex of bone.


Overview
Benign vascular tumors result from an abnormal proliferation of blood vessels and may
form around the time of birth. Historically, these tumors were called hemangiomas;
however, because of uncertainty with regard to their origin, they also can be called
vascular malformations. They rarely are found in the appendicular skeleton (pelvis and
long bones) and are more common in the axial skeleton (spine and skull). A tumor
composed of lymphatic tissues is called a lymphangioma.
Epidemiology
They can arise in individuals of any age but most commonly occur in individuals aged 30 to 60
years.
Most benign vascular tumors found in long bones are solitary; however, those that involve the
vertebrae may be multifocal.

Epidemiology
Bone hemangiomas are uncommon benign bone tumors that primarily occur in the
spine. They are found in individuals aged 30 to 60 years, and their incidence is higher in
men than women.
Etiology
Genetics/etiology: no known genetic or hereditary association
Rarely, bone involvement may be observed in patients with hemangiomatosis.

Etiology

The cause of bone hemangiomas is unknown, and they are not associated with any
known genetic condition. Skeletal involvement has been observed in some patients with
hemangiomatosis (diffuse hemangiomas throughout the body).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Most bone hemangiomas are asymptomatic.
They usually are identified incidentally on imaging studies.
Occasionally, vertebral hemangiomas will have soft-tissue extension and impinge on the spinal
cord or may fracture and cause instability.
Bone hemangiomas usually are nonpainful incidental findings. They can produce pain if they
cause nerve impingement or a fracture/instability of a bone.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Long bone hemangiomas have a variable appearance, with areas of lucency and sclerosis, but
usually lack aggressive features.
Vertebral hemangiomas may have a characteristic striated appearance with vertical sclerotic
lines (Figure 1).

so-called corduroy sign.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
T1-weighted MRIs will reveal areas of high signal intensity that most likely are fat; T2-weighted
MRIs will reveal areas of high signal intensity that most likely are blood products (Figure 3).

Imaging Studies
Bone hemangioma on plain radiographs usually is indicated by a prominent coarse
trabeculae pattern (honeycomb appearance). On coronal/sagittal CT scans, this pattern,
called the corduroy sign or the accordion sign, is more notable and occurs because
thickened trabeculae appear vertically oriented. The polka dots sign is the axial CT scan
equivalent of the corduroy sign. Bone hemangiomas will produce a high signal intensity
on T1- and T2-weighted MRI because of high fat and blood (water) products, respectively.
MRI is the best imaging modality to evaluate for neural impingement and extraosseous
extension.
Pathology
The two most common types are capillary and cavernous.
Most bone hemangiomas are composed of small (capillary) and large (cavernous) vessels in
variable proportions.


Pathology
Capillary and cavernous hemangiomas are the most common histologic types found in
bone. The capillary type consists of small vessels and capillaries, and the cavernous type
consists of large, thin-walled vessels.
Differential Diagnosis
Bone lymphangioma
Bone hemangioma and lymphangioma are radiographically similar.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Most bone hemangiomas are asymptomatic; however, if the bone lesion is symptomatic or if
the diagnosis is uncertain, a biopsy may be required to determine the correct diagnosis.
Almost all vertebral hemangiomas are asymptomatic and usually are incidental to back pain.
Observation is recommended.
Several nonsurgical treatment options include percutaneous cement vertebroplasty, radiation
therapy, sclerotherapy, and/or embolization.

Techniques/Procedures
If the diagnosis is confirmed on imaging studies, observation is recommended initially if
the bone hemangioma is asymptomatic; however, if symptomatic, several nonsurgical
treatment options exist, and injecting the lesion with bone cement (vertebroplasty) also
is effective. In addition, sclerotherapy and embolization have been used as adjuvant and
definitive treatment options for vertebral hemangiomas. Historically, radiation therapy
has been used for initial management but is no longer recommended.

Surgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
For long bone and nonvertebral hemangiomas, curettage of the lesion and grafting to prevent
fracture and control progression may be very effective.
Occasional vertebral hemangiomas with epidural extension require management. Surgical
decompression with or without external beam irradiation may be performed. Radiation
therapy should be reserved for recurrent, inoperable, or refractory cases.
Vertebral hemangiomas that result in fracture and instability often require surgical
management (rare occurrence).

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical management of bone hemangiomas rarely is required. In the appendicular
skeleton, surgical management may be warranted if the lesion is painful or at risk for
fracture. Indications for surgical management include vertebral hemangioma, pain,
nerve impingement, or risk of vertebral fracture.
